rationale: Under Biden's Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule, Israel was explicitly placed in the intermediate 'Tier 2' bucket (50,000-chip/year cap, 2025-2027) alongside Saudi Arabia/UAE -- NOT in the 18-country Tier 1 closest-ally list. That rule was rescinded 13 May 2025 before its 15 May compliance date, so the cap never took effect. On 11-12 Dec 2025 Israel became a founding signatory of the US-led 'Pax Silica' declaration (with the US, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, UK, Australia, later UAE), and on 16 Jan 2026 became the first country to sign a bilateral AI joint declaration with the US. Israeli press (CTech) frames this as 'unrestricted' silicon/model flow among members. Scored 4 rather than 5 because no equivalent BIS Federal Register Country-Group rule change specifically for Israel (like the UAE's July 2026 A:5 upgrade) was found in this pass -- the strongest 'license-free, no barriers' language traces to a single Israeli financial-tech outlet's characterization of a political declaration, not a confirmed EAR regulatory text change.

tier_label: No longer comprehensively embargoed (removed from Country Group E in Sept 2025), but still Country Group D:5 for advanced computing/chips specifically -- license required, no bilateral AI framework
source_name: BIS Press Release -- Commerce Eases Export Controls on Syria (Sept 2, 2025); K&L Gates -- US Significantly Relaxes Sanctions and Export Control Restrictions on Syria; Baker McKenzie -- BIS Clarifies D:5 Advanced Computing License Requirements Remain in Force (May 31, 2026)
rationale: Genuinely fast-moving, two-sided picture. On the relief side: Executive Order 14312 (30 June 2025) revoked the bulk of US sanctions on Syria; OFAC lifted the comprehensive Syria sanctions program effective 26 August 2025; a BIS final rule effective 2 September 2025 moved Syria OUT of the comprehensively-embargoed Country Group E and created License Exception Syria Peace and Prosperity (SPP), giving EAR99 items and several license exceptions a presumption of approval for civil/commercial end-uses; Congress repealed the Caesar Act via the FY2026 NDAA on 18 December 2025. On the restriction side: Syria remains listed in Country Group D:5, and BIS guidance dated 31 May 2026 explicitly confirmed a license is STILL required for advanced computing items (AI chips) to any entity headquartered in Syria, unaffected by the broader sanctions relief. Syria also remains a US arms-embargoed destination under ITAR. Net assessment: this project's rubric defines tier 0 as 'Country Group D:5 equivalent,' and Syria's D:5 status for exactly the chip/advanced-computing items this rubric measures was independently reaffirmed as recently as five months before this research pass -- so tier 0 remains the technically correct call despite the historic broader-sanctions turnaround. Medium rather than High confidence because primary BIS.gov/Federal Register text could not be directly fetched this session; this rests on convergent, dated secondary reporting from multiple law firms plus a BIS press-release headline.

tier_label: Comprehensively restricted -- near-total OFAC/ITSR embargo plus BIS license-required-for-virtually-all-CCL-items regime
source_name: BIS -- Iran export controls (country guidance page); eCFR 15 CFR 746.7 (Iran)
rationale: OFAC's Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR Part 560) impose a near-comprehensive embargo on Iran, and 15 CFR 746.7 requires a BIS license for virtually all Commerce Control List items exported or reexported to Iran, with a general policy of denial for most dual-use and advanced-computing categories. This is the closest real-world match to a Country Group D:5-equivalent floor case in this project's rubric -- the same tier as Cuba/North Korea/Syria. Direct fetches of bis.gov and ecfr.gov were blocked by this session's network policy; the classification rests on search-engine-surfaced excerpts of those same primary texts plus corroborating secondary legal summaries, not a direct read of the current Federal Register text.

tier_label: De facto floor case -- elevated Country Group D:1 national-security classification (2020) compounded by FTO designation of the de facto authority controlling the majority-population north
source_name: Steptoe -- Commerce Expands US Export Controls on Russia and Yemen; Baker McKenzie -- US Redesignates Ansarallah as a Foreign Terrorist Organization
rationale: BIS moved Yemen from Country Group B into the more restrictive Country Group D:1 in Feb 2020, citing national-security/transshipment concerns -- already stricter than the D:1/D:5-unclassified baseline most GCC states in this dataset sit in. Separately, in March 2025 the US redesignated Ansarallah (the Houthis, who control Sana'a and the majority of Yemen's population, and who also control Yemen's key telecom operators per multiple 2025-2026 sources) as a Foreign Terrorist Organization, layering Iran-style near-comprehensive prohibitions over any dealings with the de facto authority over most of the country's population and its telecom infrastructure. The internationally recognized government in Aden is not itself comprehensively sanctioned, so this is not a clean D:5-equivalent case the way Iran is -- scored 0 as a judgment call reflecting Yemen's split sovereignty and the practical absence of any realistic AI-chip trade channel to either authority, not a confirmed formal BIS D:5 designation. This should be re-verified against BIS's own Country Group table, which this session could not fetch directly (bis.gov/ecfr.gov both blocked).

tier_label: De facto floor case -- SDGT-designated governing authority, frozen central bank reserves, no correspondent banking, arms embargo; not a formally confirmed Country Group D:5-equivalent classification
source_name: OFAC FAQ 928 (Do U.S. sanctions on the Taliban and the Haqqani Network prohibit trade with Afghanistan?); Treasury -- Afghanistan-Related Sanctions program page
rationale: The Taliban -- Afghanistan's governing authority -- and the Haqqani Network are Specially Designated Global Terrorists under Executive Order 13224, and roughly $7 billion of Afghan central bank assets remain frozen in US financial institutions, leaving Afghanistan with no functioning correspondent banking channel. Notably, OFAC's own FAQ states sanctions do NOT categorically prohibit US persons from exporting goods/services to Afghanistan provided the transaction doesn't involve a specifically sanctioned individual or entity (General License 15 explicitly authorizes agricultural, medical, and related trade) -- so this is legally distinct from Iran's or Cuba's comprehensive embargo, and I could not independently confirm Afghanistan's current BIS Country Group letter/number (bis.gov and the BIS Interactive Country Chart were unreachable this session). Scored 0 as a practical judgment call: with the governing authority itself sanctioned, no banking channel, a UN/US arms embargo, and the Taliban's own 2025 deliberate internet blackouts restricting the underlying digital infrastructure, there is no realistic path to AI-chip trade regardless of the technical legal classification. This is the weakest-sourced export-control call of the three countries and should be revisited with direct BIS access.
